claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Transformation of high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between composition-dependent thermodynamic instability and atomic-rearrangement kinetics.
The free-energy difference between metastable BCC and lower-energy phases provides the thermodynamic driving force for transformation.
BCC–FCC phase stability and transformation rate can correspond to the Gibbs free-energy difference between those phases.
Slow cooling provides enough time for diffusion, nucleation, and growth of lower-energy phases.
Rapid cooling limits diffusion and kinetically freezes the high-temperature BCC phase.
In a CoCrFeNiTi0.4 alloy, rapid cooling inhibits several phases, whereas sufficiently slow cooling permits all observed phases to form.
Al-containing CoCrFeNi alloys can undergo multiple phase transformations, including formation of partially ordered aluminides in a BCC solid-solution matrix.
Al has strong ordering tendencies with the transition metals in the relevant Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy family.
Slow-cooled Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will contain a larger fraction of lower-energy transformed phases than rapidly quenched material.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will remain predominantly BCC.
The transformation onset temperature will coincide with the range in which ΔG_BCC-FCC exceeds the nucleation barrier.
Cooling rate will be varied while composition, initial high-temperature state, preparation, and atmosphere are held constant.
The controlled baseline is rapid quenching, expected to minimize transformation relative to controlled slow cooling.
The proposed mechanism applies only where a thermodynamic driving force is appreciable and atomic mobility remains temperature dependent.
Cooling-rate-independent phase fractions and transformation onset temperatures would falsify the proposed kinetic-control mechanism.
